chapter: Jazz opinions, Jelly Roll and the Rhythm Club
title: Jelly Roll Morton at the Rhythm Club
summary: Morton lectured musicians at the Rhythm Club on 132nd Street and Seventh Avenue, where they hung out and jammed.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: What did people think of Scott Joplin?
Never heard him.
The ragtime piano player.
Nope.
What did musicians think of Jelly Roll Morton?
Everybody said he's the only musician that really told the truth about musicians and what was going to happen.
How so?
He'd get on the corner and we'd listen every day. He would tell guys - and that was a long time ago - you wasn't even born - what was going to happen to musicians up until -
What did he predict?

No, he'd try to teach them music. He had a blackboard in the Rhythm Club and he'd try to show them music and would tell them what would be happening about 20 or 30 years from now. He didn't lie about nothing.
What were some of the things that he said?
Oh, I can't remember them.
Why did he pick the Rhythm Club?
Well, that's where all the musicians hang out... That's 132nd Street and Seventh Avenue. It's still there.
Up on the second floor?
No, it's first floor.
What kind of a club was it, organization was it?
They had a poolroom and then they had a blackboard up there and you could bring your horn in and jam.
They had piano in there?
And then you could gamble.
Had a piano and everything?
Oh, yes.
It was like a private club then?
It wasn't private. Open, anybody could come in.
Who opened the place?
Ray Howell. It was around the corner at first but it wasn't big enough. They had it in the basement then. It's still open now.
Do you know how it started? Did it start after you were in New York?
How it started? No, it was open when I came to New York.
And you just used to congregate there?
They changed it from downstairs, to upstairs on the ground floor. JCH and horn.
